questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
o: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authentication decides what you may do; authorization proves who you are
They are two names for the same login step
Authentication is for services while authorization is for people
questions.w: Authenticate first (identity), then authorize (permissions). Mixing them up is a classic interview slip.

questions.q: A logged-in user changes the id in `/accounts/1001` to `/accounts/1002` and sees someone else's account. Which flaw is this?
o: Broken object-level authorization (IDOR)
A weak password policy on the login form
Missing HTTPS on the account page
SQL injection in the account lookup query
questions.w: The user was authenticated but the server never checked that account 1002 belongs to them. Check ownership on every object access.

questions.q: Which HTTP status means "I don't know who you are"?
o: 401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
questions.w: 401 means not authenticated (or bad credentials). 403 means authenticated but not allowed.

questions.q: Why are passwords stored with a slow, salted hash such as bcrypt or Argon2 rather than plain SHA-256?
o: A slow salted hash makes guessing expensive and hides repeated passwords
SHA-256 cannot be computed on an application server
Hashes can be decrypted later if the user forgets the password
A slow hash shortens the value stored in the database
questions.w: Fast hashes let attackers test billions of guesses per second. A per-user salt defeats rainbow tables and a tunable work factor keeps cracking expensive.

questions.q: In RBAC, how are permissions granted?
o: Permissions are attached to roles and users are assigned roles
Each user is given individual permissions and nothing else
Permissions depend only on the IP address of the request
Roles are checked once at login and never again
questions.w: RBAC groups permissions into roles such as TELLER or AUDITOR. ABAC goes further and decides using attributes such as amount, time or department.

o: Proof from two or more categories: know, have, are
Two different passwords instead of one password
A longer session timeout after the first login
Encryption applied to the login page itself
questions.w: Two passwords are still one factor. Combine knowledge (password), possession (phone or token) and inherence (biometric).

questions.q: Where should authorization checks for an API be enforced?
o: On the server for every request, whatever the UI hides
Only in the front end, by hiding the buttons
Only once at login time, when the token is issued
Only in the gateway's routing table at deploy time
questions.w: Anyone can call the API directly. Hiding a button is UX, not security. Enforce on the server, ideally close to the data.

questions.q: A session cookie should be marked `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite`. What does `HttpOnly` prevent?
o: JavaScript cannot read the cookie, limiting theft through XSS
The cookie is never sent over plain HTTP connections
Other sites cannot attach the cookie to cross-site requests
The browser deletes the cookie when the tab is closed
questions.w: `Secure` limits it to HTTPS and `SameSite` reduces CSRF. `HttpOnly` hides it from `document.cookie`.
